citation: README.md desiderata, agent states are the point and attention routing; docs/architecture.md, ownership of truth and one action path
why: The list is what makes agent states glanceable, so the decisions it carries are what somebody sees before they see anything else: which tabs there are, in what order, what each row is called, and which chord reaches it. A chord is the presses in order, and it is a property of the arrangement rather than of the gesture: the same row carries the same chord whether or not a press is outstanding, so a pane in a tab nobody is looking at can be addressed without pressing anything first (kan a_2LSUoy7dd). Tab, then pane - a flat list of panes cannot say which of them sit side by side, and a window shows one tab at a time, so the tab is what a person navigates between. The machine is not a level of it, because a tab may hold panes on two (MIP-2): it goes on the pane row, and a machine holding no panes at all is in the machines list, which is the only place that state can be said. Ordering and labelling are here rather than in the shell so that the sidebar, the CLI and an agent cannot each make their own answer.

cases.why: The list runs down the side of a window whose panes run across it, and the eye moves between the two constantly. Sorting by id instead would be stable and would disagree with the screen for any tab somebody has rearranged, which is every tab after the first split.

cases.name: a pane is named by its directory and the harness in it
cases.why:
The two things that tell coding-agent panes apart when nobody has said otherwise. The id says nothing to anybody; the directory answers 'which project' and the harness answers 'which of these is running claude', which are the two questions a list like this gets asked.

This used to argue that a terminal title is whatever the program last felt like setting, and therefore worth nothing. That was wrong about coding agents, which set it to what they are working on, and it is now the second line of the row. It stays off the first line for the reason the old wording was reaching for: a title changes as work happens, and the line you learn a pane by should not.

cases.why:
What `muster focus --place 3` means: the pane `muster window` prints at place 3. Counting from one rather than zero because the sidebar counts that way, and down the whole window rather than within a tab because a script reads the number off `muster window` and hands it back, so it has to mean what it was read as - whatever the numbered chords are naming at the time.

cases.name: an agent's own title is the second line of its row
cases.why:
The founding promise is that fifteen agents can be told apart at a glance, and fifteen rows reading `<directory> · claude` cannot do it: they say where a session lives, never what it is doing. A harness already publishes what it is doing as its terminal title, so nothing has to be invented - only carried and drawn.

In the core rather than in the sidebar because it is a decision, and the CLI and an agent asking what the window holds must get the same answer as the person reading it.

cases.name: a pane with no harness gets no second line, whatever it calls itself
cases.why:
A shell sets a title too. oh-my-zsh's default is `<user>@<host>:<path>`, which is the row's own first line spelled longer, and most panes in a window are a shell somebody left open - so a rule of 'draw it when it exists' would double the height of the list to repeat it.

Requiring a detected harness is a fact the daemon reports, where suppressing shell titles by shape would be a guess about somebody's dotfiles. The cost is real and is accepted here rather than hidden: a pane running something that titles itself usefully, in which the daemon recognized no agent, stays on one line.

Compared against the label, the directory, the whole path and the harness, because a title matching any of them is a title the reader has already read.

cases.name: a name somebody gave a pane replaces the directory and the harness
cases.why:
A person running fifteen agents wants to say which is which in their own words. Their name wins over anything derived because it is the only line here that was written for this pane rather than worked out from where it happens to be - and it is the durable one: the daemon writes a name down, so it survives a daemon restart, where the directory and the harness are re-derived each time.

The raw text travels beside the label so that asking to rename can start from what was typed rather than from a composed label nobody chose.

cases.why: The chords name places in this list, so the order it is built in is the order ⌘1 to ⌘9 reach. Ids are opaque strings the backend spells - `w1:t1`, `w1:t10` - and sorting them is numeric order right up until there are ten of something, at which point `w1:t10` lands between `w1:t1` and `w1:t2`. The order is the one the backend listed rather than one derived from the id, which is why this case states its tabs in order and expects them back in it.

cases.name: a window of one tab numbers its panes
cases.why:
With one tab a first press carries no information: ⌘1 names the only tab there is, and reaching its second pane costs ⌘1 ⌘2. So a window holding one tab numbers panes, one press each - a pane's place down the whole window and its place inside that tab are the same number here.

Both presses are pinned, and that is the half worth pinning. Counting `panes` rather than `panes in local/w1:t1` is what says no chord is half-typed: the shell draws a number over every pane while one is and ends the gesture when the modifier comes up, so a numbering that said panes-inside-a-tab here would leave those numbers drawn forever with nothing having been pressed. Two presses in a row reaching the same pane is what that reads as.

The trigger is one tab in the window rather than one tab on the machine holding the keyboard. Per machine the same key would mean different things depending which column the keyboard sat in, with nothing on screen changing as it moved; per window the meaning changes only when a second tab appears, and that at least moves every number in the list as it happens. kan a_2Hx68fXqr.

cases.why:
The keyboard has nine numbered chords and this tab holds ten panes, so the tenth has no second press. What matters is what it carries instead: nothing at all, rather than the ⌘2 that reaches its tab. ⌘2 lands on that tab's *first* pane, so a row drawing ⌘2 beside the tenth would be a keystroke that looks like it goes there and goes somewhere else - worse than a row with no address, because there is nothing to notice.

The rule belongs to the chord rather than to either press: a chord with a press missing is not an address. That is also what a pane in a tab past the ninth carries - neither press, because nothing reaches its tab to begin with.

cases.why: What stage four of MIP-2 is for, seen from the list. One tab, one caption, and its panes from both machines under it in the order their regions sit - which is why the machine goes on the pane row: the tab cannot say it, because for this tab there is no single answer.

cases.name: a pane can be compacted when its daemon says its agent compacts
cases.why: The agent row's menu offers Compact Agent and greys it out where nothing would be typed: a pane running no agent, or an agent whose manifest gives no compact line. The daemon is the one that types it, from the manifests it holds, so the row carries the daemon's word rather than a guess made from the app's own manifests.

cases.name: a hidden tab is listed apart, unnumbered, and quiet panes say so
cases.why: A hidden pane is one somebody put out of sight with its agent still running. No window shows it and no chord reaches it, so it takes no place in the window's order - numbering it would shift every chord below it - and is listed apart so that what its agent is doing stays in view and it can be brought back. Quiet is said on every row, hidden or not, because a menu offers to take it back.

cases.name: a helper's row names the pane that made it, wherever the helper is held
cases.why: A helper is a pane another pane's agent made for its own work (MIP-7). Its daemon keeps which pane that was, and every row carries it, so whatever lists helpers under their maker reads it off the row rather than guessing from tabs or names. A helper beside its maker and a hidden one carry it alike, and a pane nobody made carries none.

cases.name: a hidden helper is listed under a maker that has a row, and a shown one keeps its place
cases.why: The list shows a maker's hidden helpers beneath its row rather than under Hidden (MIP-7, section 3), and says which on each helper's row, so the agent list and `muster window` follow one rule. A helper of a hidden helper goes under that helper, a row further in. A helper in a tab somebody can see keeps its place and its number there, since a row moved under its maker would put the numbers out of order. A hidden helper whose maker has no row - closed, or in another window - stays under Hidden with nothing to go beneath.

cases.name: a pane can be restarted when its daemon knows how its agent resumes
cases.why: The agent row's menu offers Restart Agent and greys it out where there is nothing to resume: a pane running no agent, or an agent that reported no session its harness resumes. The daemon builds the resume from what the agent reported and the manifests it holds, so the row carries the daemon's word, and the command it would run is what the window says before it ends anything.

cases.name: a tab interleaving two machines is numbered in its tree's reading order
cases.why: The devenv's pane sits between the laptop's two, below a and to the left of c, so it is second in the tree and second in the list. Going machine by machine would number it third, and cmd+2 would land on c, which the window draws third (MIP-8, section 5).
